value: Deciphered via the trilingual Rosetta Stone decree (196 BCE) plus the known descendant language Coptic plus royal names in cartouches (Ptolemy, Cleopatra, Ramesses, Thutmose); verified by predictive reading of previously unread cartouches and, by the 1850s, translation of continuous texts.

value: Read as the cursive Egyptian tradition ancestral to demotic; demotic signs derive from hieratic/hieroglyphic forms, and hieratic was recovered within the Egyptian decipherment sequence.

value: Deciphered largely by Young (1816 in the standard timeline) using the Rosetta Stone and other Greek-demotic parallel texts.

value: Deciphered in layers: Old Persian first from Persepolis copies and Behistun, then Akkadian via Behistun parallels and proper names; verified in 1857 when Rawlinson, Hincks, Oppert and Fox Talbot independently translated a new Tiglath-Pileser I inscription with largely coinciding results.
asserted_by: Grotefend; Rawlinson; Hincks; Oppert; Fox Talbot
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: First cuneiform variety deciphered (~36 phonetic signs): Grotefend (1802) guessed the royal formula 'X, great king, son of Y' from later Persian inscriptions; completed by Rawlinson at Behistun with Burnouf and Lassen.

value: Deciphered in 1930 within about a year: 30 signs implied an alphabet, a word-divider aided segmentation, and the language was correctly assumed to be North-West Semitic related to Phoenician/Hebrew; verified by coherent myths, letters and word-lists.
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Deciphered late: progress in the 1930s stalled while the language was assumed to be Hittite proper; the decisive step was recognising it as Luwian, aided by Luwian-Phoenician bilinguals (Karatepe, found 1946) and Laroche's sign list, with a 1970s re-reading making continuous translation routine.
asserted_by: Bossert; Laroche; Hawkins; Morpurgo Davies; Melchert
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Deciphered by Barthélemy (1758) via Greek-Phoenician bilingual coin legends and the Melqart cippi from Malta, using known Semitic cognates (Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic); verified by consistent readings across the Mediterranean corpus of 22 consonantal signs.
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Partly deciphered: Gardiner (1916) read the recurring word b'lt 'the Lady' by acrophony (a sign stands for the first sound of the Semitic word for what it depicts); outline accepted as the origin of the alphabet, but many sign values and most readings remain disputed with no bilingual.
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Deciphered without a bilingual by internal structure (Kober's triplets proving inflection; Ventris's syllabic grid) plus place-name cribs and the correct guess that the language was Greek (1952); verified predictively by newly excavated Pylos tablets, e.g. the tripod tablet Ta 641.
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Deciphered by Knorozov's reinterpretation of de Landa's 'alphabet' as syllabic signs with positional analysis using living Mayan languages, plus Proskouriakoff's non-phonetic proof from date patterns that stelae record dynastic history; verified when independent readers produce the same historical readings on new monuments (about 80-90% of Classic texts now readable).
asserted_by: Knorozov (1952-58); Proskouriakoff (1960); Berlin; Stuart; Schele; Lounsbury
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Deciphered 1871-72 via the Idalion bilingual (a Phoenician-Cypriot syllabic dedication, 4th c. BCE) plus the fact that most texts turned out to be Greek (Arcadocypriot); the syllabary of ~55 signs is derived from Cypro-Minoan.

value: Script fully readable for centuries: alphabet borrowed from Euboean Greek c. 700 BCE; the language is only partly understood, helped modestly by the parallel (not literal) Pyrgi tablets (two Etruscan, one Phoenician, c. 500 BCE).
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Northeastern Iberian semi-syllabary deciphered by Gómez-Moreno (1922) using coin legends with known place-names and Greco-Iberian bilingual material; Southeastern and Greco-Iberian scripts followed; the Iberian language itself remains not understood.
removal_condition: Superseded if the source corrects or replaces this statement.

value: Deciphered late (Ray, 1980s-90s; Adiego's corpus 2007) from Carian-Egyptian material and Carian-Greek bilinguals/graffiti of mercenaries in Egypt, showing many Greek look-alike letters have different values; a century of Greek-value readings had produced gibberish.

value: Decipherment aided by the Letoon trilingual (Lycian-Greek-Aramaic, 1973, Xanthos) and the Xanthos stele; Lycian A is well understood as Anatolian, while Lycian B (Milyan) remains only partly understood.

value: Script deciphered almost fully by de Saulcy (1843) via the Dougga (Thugga) Punic-Libyan bilingual mausoleum inscription; the language is early Berber but most short funerary texts yield little beyond names and formulae.
